abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Natural iron-rich minerals are potential low-cost alternatives for biomass direct chemical looping (BDCL) systems, but their interactions with different biomass feedstocks remain poorly understood. This study evaluated Badar stone, a volcanic iron-rich natural mineral from Indonesia, against synthetic Fe2O3 using six representative biomass feedstocks, consisting of three lignocellulosic biomasses, namely rice husk, sawdust, and sago waste, and three microalgal biomasses, namely Aurantiochytrium, Euglena, and Spirulina. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) under N2 was employed to examine devolatilization behavior and interactions between char and OC. A mass balance-based multistep kinetic model was used to assess thermal decomposition and apparent kinetic behavior across 400–800, 800–1000, and 1000–1300 K. Biomass devolatilization dominated the TG response at low and intermediate temperatures, while clearer biomass–oxygen carrier differences appeared at higher temperatures. Rice husk showed limited sensitivity to Badar stone loading, with sums of fitted apparent activation energies of 367.1–369.5 kJ/mol. Sawdust showed stronger oxygen carrier dependence, with the corresponding value decreasing from 371.1 kJ/mol with Badar stone to 307.2 kJ/mol with Fe2O3. Spirulina exhibited the highest values among the microalgal biomasses, reaching 416.2 kJ/mol with Badar stone and 429.3 kJ/mol with Fe2O3. Badar stone produced broader and more gradual high-temperature TG responses, whereas Fe2O3 produced sharper responses. These results demonstrate that the apparent thermochemical behavior depends strongly on both biomass type and oxygen carrier composition, providing a basis for selecting biomass–mineral combinations for subsequent cyclic and reactor-scale evaluation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Biomass direct chemical looping (BDCL) is a promising thermochemical approach for converting renewable biomass using lattice oxygen supplied by a solid oxygen carrier (OC). Biomass is relatively affordable to produce, readily available for feedstocks, and can be processed using simple technologies. Depending on the oxygen availability, OC loading, and operating conditions, direct contact between biomass and the OC may be applied to biomass chemical looping combustion (BCLC), which targets extensive fuel conversion into CO2 and H2O, or biomass chemical looping gasification (BCLG), which employs substoichiometric lattice oxygen to promote syngas production. In both configurations, the OC transfers lattice oxygen and heat while avoiding direct contact between the biomass and air.

The development of a suitable OC remains one of the principal technical challenges in BCLG. An effective OC should have sufficient oxygen transport capacity, appropriate lattice oxygen reactivity for partial oxidation, catalytic activity toward biomass-derived intermediates, good mechanical strength, and resistance to sintering, agglomeration, attrition, and deactivation by biomass ash. Synthetic OCs can be designed to provide high reactivity and structural stability, but their preparation commonly requires additional raw materials, support phases, and energy-intensive synthesis procedures. Natural ores offer lower material and preparation costs and are generally more readily available, although their redox performance may be affected by variations in Fe content, mineral phases, inert constituents, particle strength, and interactions with biomass ash.

Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of natural ores for biomass direct chemical looping, particularly for BCLG. Ge et al. used natural hematite for rice husk gasification in a 25 kWth reactor and demonstrated the feasibility of using an inexpensive Fe-based mineral as the OC. Condori et al. subsequently reported 55 h of continuous pine wood gasification using ilmenite in a 1.5 kWth unit, showing that the transported lattice oxygen could be controlled to regulate syngas production. Using Fe and Mn ores at the same reactor scale, Condori et al. obtained biomass and carbon conversions above 94% and 95%, respectively, although attrition and the migration of active metals toward the particle surface reduced the estimated carrier lifetime. Natural manganese ore has also been examined for rice husk gasification, revealing that OC performance is affected by interactions between the mineral and Si-rich biomass ash. Modification of iron ore with NiO was reported to improve biomass char conversion and syngas formation, although this approach introduces an additional preparation step and a more expensive active component. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the potential of natural OCs for biomass direct chemical looping while highlighting unresolved challenges related to oxygen availability, feedstock-dependent behavior, structural stability, ash interactions, and the balance between material cost and redox performance

The reaction kinetics of biomass and the OC in the fuel reactor are particularly important because they determine how well the chemical looping system operates, which products it produces, and how it is designed. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) is a commonly used method for investigating kinetic behavior, owing to its exceptional accuracy and sensitivity in detecting mass changes under controlled thermal conditions. Isoconversional or model-free methods have been widely used to determine how apparent activation energies change with conversion. This method provides a preliminary understanding of biomass decomposition; however, it frequently inadequately captures the intricate, multistage reactions that transpire within heterogeneous feedstocks. Biomass is composed of various components, including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, proteins, and lipids. Each of these parts breaks down differently when heated. Consequently, multistep or multipseudo-component kinetic models have been suggested to represent these overlapping decomposition phases more precisely.

Pseudocomponent models are limited in their ability to describe how intermediates and gaseous products change over time, even though they fit thermogravimetric data well. On the other hand, multistep kinetic schemes provide clearer mechanistic insights into how solid and volatile species are formed and broken down. The two-step first-order kinetic model, first proposed by Di Blasi and Lanzetta (1997), has been widely used to predict how biomass loses weight in both isothermal and nonisothermal conditions, such as isothermal conditions for cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin and isothermal conditions of poplar wood by Silveira et al. Nonetheless, the application of these models to nonisothermal processes, such as temperature-programmed reactions, is problematic because the temperature dependence of rate constants varies. Thus, sophisticated numerical algorithms are essential for the efficient determination of reliable kinetic parameters. ,

Previous studies have primarily examined synthetic Fe2O3, conventional iron ores, sludge-derived carriers, or other established oxygen carrier (OC) systems, as shown in Table , frequently using a limited number of biomass feedstocks. Systematic comparisons across both lignocellulosic and microalgal biomasses under a common kinetic framework remain limited. In addition, geological provenance has received relatively little attention as a material selection perspective for identifying unexplored natural Fe-rich minerals, although geological origin itself should not be interpreted as evidence of superior redox behavior. For instance, Fe2O3-rich sludge ash reduced the activation energy in the high-temperature zone (HTZ) during pine sawdust pyrolysis, while Fe2O3 addition significantly increased CO2 yield and gas conversion in low-ash coal gasification systems. Similar findings were reported for corn straw and lignin, where isoconversional and Malek analyses revealed transitions from chemical reaction to diffusion-controlled regimes. In nonisothermal studies, Fe2O3-based OCs consistently followed multistage reduction sequences (Fe2O3→Fe3O4→FeO→Fe), with activation energies typically ranging between 90 and 200 kJ·mol–1 depending on feedstock composition and C/O ratio. , Notably, kinetic modeling using multistep schemes (e.g., D1 or C1.5 models) has shown that OCs not only modify activation energy but also alter product distributions and intermediate yields. These findings collectively demonstrate that natural or synthetic Fe-based carriers strongly influence biomass conversion pathways and can be rationally selected to balance reactivity, selectivity, and stability.

sec.p: Despite growing interest in natural Fe-based OCs, most previous studies have focused on established materials such as conventional iron ores, ilmenite, and iron sand, whereas geological provenance has rarely been explicitly considered in identifying new OC candidates. Volcanic and subvolcanic geological systems can generate or concentrate Fe-bearing phases through several processes, including magmatic segregation, iron oxide-apatite mineralization, hydrothermal alteration, and the weathering and placer accumulation of volcanic rocks. Fe-rich materials associated with these environments include Kiruna-type apatite iron oxide ores, the magnetite-rich El Laco volcanic system, , several iron oxide-apatite deposits in Chile and Armenia, , and titanomagnetite iron sands derived from volcanic rocks in New Zealand and Indonesia. , These examples demonstrate that volcanic-related geological environments can host materials with substantial Fe contents that warrant investigation for thermochemical applications. However, volcanic origin alone does not establish superior redox performance and should instead be regarded as an underexplored perspective for identifying potential natural OCs.

Within this context, Badar stone (Figure ) was selected as a locally available Fe-rich natural material from Pati, Central Java, Indonesia. Geological studies associate Badar stone with jasper-type formations developed in a submarine volcanic environment. Such materials may form through interactions between basaltic lava and unconsolidated wet sediment, followed by hydrothermal alteration and silicification, and are commonly associated with basalt lava and hyaloclastite breccia. The raw material was initially goethite-rich and transformed predominantly into hematite after calcination, while elemental analysis showed that Fe was the dominant element at 59.7 wt %. Together with its naturally heterogeneous mineral composition, these characteristics provide a rational basis for its initial evaluation as a potential natural OC. Therefore, the selection of Badar stone does not rely solely on its previously unexplored status, nor does the present study assume that it outperforms established natural ores or synthetic Fe2O3.

sec.p: However, the thermogravimetric behavior and apparent kinetic behavior of Badar stone in biomass conversion remain unexplored. Therefore, this study investigates Badar stone as a potential natural OC under conditions relevant to reduction in the fuel reactor and compares its response with that of synthetic Fe2O3. Six representative biomass feedstocks were selected to cover distinct biochemical and ash characteristics, namely rice husk (RH), sawdust (SD), and sago waste (SW), as lignocellulosic biomasses, and Aurantiochytrium (MA), Euglena (ME), and Spirulina (MS), as microalgal biomasses. The lignocellulosic feedstocks are primarily composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, whereas the microalgal feedstocks contain different proportions of lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates. These compositional differences are expected to produce distinct devolatilization and residual solid behaviors. The objective is to determine how biomass composition, OC loading, and OC type influence the net thermogravimetric response and fitted apparent kinetic parameters. Because gaseous products were not analyzed, the experiments are not used to distinguish complete combustion from syngas-oriented gasification or to demonstrate reactor-scale BCLC or BCLG performance.

sec.p: The proximate and ultimate analyses of the six biomass feedstocks are summarized in Table . Prior to the TGA experiments, Badar stone was calcined in an air atmosphere at a heating rate of 10 °C/min to 600 °C, then the rate was decreased to 5 °C/min until the temperature reached 1,000 °C, and held for 12 h to improve its reactivity and mechanical strength. Badar stone was dried at room temperature to remove humidity, then crushed and sieved to 80–200 μm. In addition, α-Fe2O3 (Wako Pure Chemical Industries, Ltd., 99.9%) was employed as OC for comparison.

caption.title: Characterization of Biomass Used in This Study

sec.p: X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using a Rigaku MiniFlex 600 to analyze the crystalline structure of the samples. The XRD data were collected at a continuous scan rate of 5 °/min over a 2θ range of 10° to 80°. The XRD patterns were background corrected, mildly smoothed for visualization, and normalized to facilitate comparison among samples. The processing did not alter the original peak positions. As shown in Figure , the raw Badar stone contained goethite together with Fe2O3-bearing phases, with further details provided in Figure S.1 of the Supporting Information. After calcination, the material transformed into a predominantly hematite (Fe2O3), as indicated by the characteristic diffraction peaks at 24°, 33°, 36°, 41°, 49°, 54°, 62°, and 64°. The synthetic Fe2O3 reference material was also characterized by XRD to establish its initial crystalline phase and ensure a rigorous basis for comparison with calcined Badar stone. In addition to phase identification, elemental composition was analyzed using ICP–SFMS (Inductively Coupled Plasma Sector Field Mass Spectrometry) conducted by an external accredited laboratory (ALS Scandinavia, Sweden). The reported uncertainty represents the extended measurement uncertainty provided by the laboratory at an approximately 95% confidence level. Because ICP–SFMS quantified selected metallic elements and did not directly determine oxygen, the reported elemental concentrations are not expected to sum to 100%. The elemental analysis results summarized in Table show that iron is the dominant element in Badar stone, consistent with the XRD results and confirming the hematite-rich nature of the material.

sec.title: Experimental Setup
sec.p: In a typical test, N2 at a flow rate of 500 mL/min was used as an inert purge gas to prevent oxidation by ambient air, in accordance with the operating requirements of the Rigaku thermogravimetric instrument. The purge gas was introduced from the rear of the furnace system and was not directed as a high-velocity jet onto the sample surface. The same gas-flow condition was consistently applied to all experiments. Biomass and OC were weighed separately and manually mixed using a mortar and pestle prior to each run to promote a uniform distribution of the two solid components. Subsequently, 5 mg of biomass was tested either alone as the biomass-only control or physically mixed with 2.5, 5, or 10 mg of Badar stone, corresponding to OC-to-biomass mass ratios of 0.5, 1, and 2, respectively. Comparative experiments using synthetic Fe2O3 were conducted at an OC-to-biomass mass ratio of 1. The biomass loading of 5 mg was selected to maintain a shallow, reproducible sample bed and to ensure that all biomass and OC mixtures remained within the crucible’s practical volumetric capacity, particularly for low-bulk-density feedstocks such as sawdust. Prior to each TGA experiment, the separately weighed biomass and OC were manually mixed using a mortar and pestle to promote a uniform distribution of the two solid components. The mixture was then transferred directly into the TGA sample holder. The same mixing procedure was consistently applied to all experimental conditions. The sample was first heated from room temperature to 383 at 20 K/min and held for 10 min to remove moisture, followed by heating to 1300 K at the same rate. Because no external reducing gas was supplied during these runs, the measured mass loss reflects biomass pyrolysis and the subsequent interaction of pyrolysis-derived gases and char with the OC under TGA conditions. Therefore, the present nonisothermal TGA experiments are interpreted as a comparative kinetic screening tool rather than as a direct representation of reactor-scale chemical looping behavior. In addition, selected experimental conditions were independently repeated to evaluate the run-to-run repeatability of the TG and DTG profiles. The repeated experiments were selected to cover lignocellulosic and microalgal biomass samples, biomass-only controls, different Badar stone loadings, and synthetic Fe2O3 comparisons. For each repeated experiment, the biomass and OC were separately weighed, manually mixed, and transferred to the TGA sample holder following the same preparation and operating procedures. Repeatability was quantitatively assessed using pairwise RMSE values calculated from the normalized TG profiles. Representative TG and DTG overlays and the corresponding repeatability metrics are provided in Table S.1 of the Supporting Information. The replicate set was designed to evaluate the technical repeatability of representative experimental conditions rather than to provide statistical replication for every biomass and OC combination. Because parameter-specific fitting uncertainty was not independently determined, small differences of only a few kJ/mol among the fitted apparent activation energies are considered comparable and are not interpreted as evidence of distinctly different reaction mechanisms.

The governing equations were numerically integrated in MATLAB R2024b using ODE45, which is an explicit Runge–Kutta (4,5) solver with adaptive step size control. The objective function was minimized using fmincon as a constrained local optimizer to estimate the apparent kinetic parameters (Ai, Ei) and the fitted solid allocation parameter (α i). To reduce dependence on initial guesses, multiple initial parameter sets were tested, and the solution with the lowest objective function value was retained. Microscale TGA does not reproduce the hydrodynamic and solid–gas contacting conditions of a larger reactor. Accordingly, the fitted kinetic parameters are interpreted as apparent descriptors of the nonisothermal TG response under the selected experimental conditions, rather than as intrinsic kinetic constants completely independent of heat and mass transfer effects.

sec.title: Thermogravimetric Analysis
sec.p: The TGA and differential thermogravimetric (DTG) analyses results for all biomass samples, along with their mixtures with Badar stone and synthetic hematite (Fe2O3) at ratios of 0.5, 1, and 2, are presented in Figure . The biomass-only condition, without any OC, served as the control for evaluating changes associated with OC addition. The corresponding difference TG curves, normalized by the initial biomass mass, are provided in Figure S.4 of the Supporting Information. The highest decomposition peaks were observed at 595, 540, and 600 K for RH, SD, and SW, respectively, and at 570, 590, and 593 K for MA, ME, and MS, respectively. Unlike the other microalgae, MA exhibited a distinct secondary DTG peak at approximately 670 K, indicating an additional devolatilization stage associated with its higher lipid fraction.

sec.p: The decomposition of pure lignocellulosic-based biomass showed multiple degradation zones corresponding to the devolatilization of hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin, which align with their characteristic biochemical compositions. For RH, the major fractions were cellulose (35.86%), lignin (24.52%), and hemicellulose (18.20%). SW contained approximately 39.5% cellulose, 10.35% lignin, and 17.8% hemicellulose, while Sengon SD comprised 48.98 wt % cellulose, 26.66 wt % lignin, and 23.33 wt % hemicellulose

In the case of lignocellulosic-based biomass blended with Badar stone or Fe2O3, initial devolatilization occurred between 500 and 800 K. The presence of Badar or Fe2O3 had a limited effect on primary volatile release but a greater influence on possible interaction among residual char, pyrolysis-derived gases, and OC interactions at higher temperatures (950–1100 K), similar to the reported cellulose–Fe2O3 reactivity. Hemicellulose decomposed over a lower but broader temperature range (490–690 K) with two DTG peaks, which can be clearly observed in RH and is attributed to glycosidic bond cleavage and side-chain fragmentation. In SW and SD, the characteristic double peak does not appear, mainly due to the substantially lower cellulose and hemicellulose intensities. As shown by Sun and Aziz, the peak intensities of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin are approximately −90, −30, and −10 mg/K, respectively; however, in RH, the very high ash content enhances the distinction of the two hemicellulose-related peaks, making them more visible in the DTG profile. Lignocellulosic-based biomass exhibited overlapping peaks due to the combined degradation of all three components, while lignin contributed to a wider thermal span up to 850 K, characterized by β-O-4 bond cleavage near 630 K. At elevated temperatures (990–1100 K), additional mass loss was observed in the lignocellulosic-based biomass–OC mixtures. Under the present TGA conditions, this behavior is more cautiously interpreted as being associated with interactions between biomass-derived char and pyrolysis-derived gases with the OC, rather than being assigned exclusively to a specific iron oxide reduction pathway. This interpretation is consistent with previous observations for lignin–Fe2O3 blends.

The decomposition of microalgal-based biomass exhibited distinct devolatilization behaviors, governed by its biochemical composition, which differ markedly from those of lignocellulosic feedstocks. Microalgae devolatilization primarily resulted from the thermal degradation of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins. For MA, the proximate biochemical composition consisted of approximately 22.60% protein and 64.00% lipids, with negligible carbohydrates. ME exhibited 17.8–23.2% protein, 6.1–9.8% lipids, and 63.7–71.1% carbohydrates, whereas MS was characterized by a high protein content of 55–70%, a moderate lipid fraction of 6–9%, and a carbohydrate range of 15–25%.

The first DTG peak between 550 and 600 K corresponds to protein denaturation and polysaccharide decomposition, while the secondary peak near 670 K observed for MA is attributed to lipid cracking and long-chain hydrocarbon release, consistent with its higher lipid content compared to ME and MS. A broad high-temperature region above 700 K was associated with the gradual decomposition of residual carbonaceous materials and fixed carbon, which devolatilized slowly up to around 1100 K. , These results indicate that microalgal-based biomass exhibits more complex devolatilization behavior than lignocellulosic biomass due to the coexistence of nitrogenous and lipid-rich compounds. Unlike other microalgae, ME has a deep mass reduction and similar to protein- and carbohydrate-rich biomasses such as defatted Chlorella, because its thermolytic degradation occurs predominantly between 500–600 K, where intense volatilization of intracellular organics (proteins, polysaccharides, and residual lipids) takes place, leading to rapid devolatilization and release of gases such as CO2, CO, CH4, and light hydrocarbons. A 1:1 Fe2O3 ratio showed higher reduction performance than an equivalent Badar stone ratio and exhibited behavior comparable to the 2:1 Badar mixture, highlighting both the catalytic advantage and the inherent limitations of pure Fe2O3.

To support the temperature-based interpretation, three thermal zones were defined for the subsequent kinetic analysis, namely LTZ (400–800 K), MTZ (800–1000 K), and HTZ (1000–1300 K). These zones were selected to separate the main thermal regimes observed in the TG and DTG profiles. Previous studies reported that the reduction of Fe2O3-based oxygen carriers may undergo stepwise reduction from Fe2O3 to Fe3O4, Fe3O4 to FeO, and FeO to Fe within overlapping temperature ranges. Ubando et al. reported that in microalgae chemical looping, Fe2O3 is reduced to Fe3O4 within 638–828 K, followed by Fe3O4 to FeO at 868–1073 K, and finally FeO to Fe above 1073 K. Similarly, Robles et al. found that for forest residue biochar, reduction proceeds from Fe2O3→Fe3O4 at 837–923 K, Fe3O4→FeO at 923–1004 K, and FeO→Fe above 1004 K. Wang et al. conducted sawdust–Fe2O3 reduction experiments, showing that the stepwise reduction occurred from Fe2O3→Fe3O4 at approximately 973 K, followed by Fe3O4→FeO between 1023–1073 K, and finally FeO→Fe at 1123–1173 K. However, in the present study, the LTZ, MTZ, and HTZ are used as empirical fitting windows to separate distinct regions of the measured TG and DTG profiles and should not be interpreted as mechanistically exclusive reaction regimes or as one-to-one assignments of individual iron oxide reduction steps. In the LTZ and much of the MTZ, biomass devolatilization provides the dominant contribution to the observed net mass loss, as indicated by the major DTG peaks and the relatively limited separation among different OC loadings. Nevertheless, simultaneous oxygen carrier reduction, carbon deposition, secondary reactions involving pyrolysis-derived species, char formation, and other overlapping processes cannot be excluded. Therefore, the fitted parameters represent apparent descriptors of the net thermogravimetric response within each temperature window rather than intrinsic kinetic parameters of a single rate-controlling mechanism.

To clarify the main thermal transformation reactions within each zone, Table summarizes the temperature ranges for the main chemical and structural transformations of biomass components based on the literature. Microalgae biomass contains mainly carbohydrate, lipid, and protein fractions. Moisture and volatile organics are present in all types. In the LTZ, dehydration and devolatilization occur alongside the decomposition of hemicellulose and a portion of cellulose. In the MTZ, cellulose and lignin decomposition together with char formation are expected to dominate the overall mass loss, while OC reduction may begin to contribute. In the HTZ, the clearer mass-loss differences among OC ratios suggest stronger interactions between residual char or pyrolysis-derived gases and OC.

sec.p: In addition, the relatively similar TG trends observed between 800 and 1000 K are consistent with the chemical looping experiments on corn straw reported by Yan et al. The separate TG–DTA tests shown in Figure provide additional context regarding the temperature-dependent reduction behavior of Badar stone and synthetic Fe2O3. Under the gas-fuel conditions used in these separate tests, reactions with CO and H2 became more evident near 800 K, whereas CH4 required higher temperatures. However, these gas-fuel experiments should not be interpreted as evidence that OC reduction is absent below 1000 K during the biomass experiments. Rather, the limited separation among the biomass–OC TG profiles suggests that biomass-derived transformations provide the dominant contribution to the net mass change in the LTZ and much of the MTZ, while oxygen carrier reduction, carbon deposition, and secondary reactions may simultaneously contribute.

sec.title: Apparent Kinetic Behavior from the Multistep Fitting Model
sec.p: Based on the two-step reaction kinetics, the model fittings of all samples at LTZ, MTZ, and HTZ are shown in Figures and , and the corresponding kinetic parameters are listed in Tables S.2 to S.4 of the Supporting Information. The range of the pre-exponential factor (A) and activation energy (E) was 103–1021 and e1–e7, respectively, in the model fitting process. In summary, the two-step kinetic model was demonstrated to attain high fitting quality; for instance, the fitting qualities of lignocellulosic-based biomass at LTZ were within the range of 99.28%–99.93%, while in MTZ the range of 99.96% to 99.99%, and HTZ is 99.14% and 99.96%, while of microalgal-based biomass at LTZ were within the range of 97.86%–99.88%, while in MTZ the range of 99.96% to 99.99%, and HTZ is 99.75% and 99.96%, The low fit is occurs in ME at LTZ, mainly due to the sudden drop in the volatilization of ME, as shown in Figure b.

Experimental and fitted TG profiles for microalgal biomasses at different OC ratios.

sec.p: The high fitting quality indicates that the selected mathematical structure can adequately describe the measured TG response under the present nonisothermal condition. However, the fitted parameters should be interpreted as apparent kinetic parameters rather than intrinsic kinetic constants of individual elementary reactions. This distinction is important because the TG curves reflect overlapping processes of biomass decomposition, volatile release, residual char transformation, and possible interactions with the mineral phase. Therefore, the two-step model is used here as a comparative tool to identify differences among biomass and mineral combinations, not as a direct mechanistic proof of each individual reaction pathway.

The apparent activation energies of each biomass, OC ratio, and zone for lignocellulosic-based and microalgal-based biomass are depicted in Figure a and c, respectively. For compact comparison, ΣEa represents the sum of the fitted apparent activation energies of the sequential steps and is interpreted only as a model-based comparative descriptor, rather than as a single physical activation barrier. The individual fitted apparent activation energies for each sequential step are provided in Tables S.2 to S.4 in the Supporting Information. The kinetic differences between LTZ and MTZ remained minimal across mixing ratios. This behavior is fully consistent with devolatilization-controlled regimes. This behavior is consistent with the TG and DTG results, in which the main mass loss below 1000 K is driven by biomass devolatilization.

sec.p: In the LTZ, the mass loss may be dominated by the release of moisture, light volatiles, and the decomposition of easily degradable biomass components. For lignocellulosic biomass, this includes hemicellulose and part of cellulose decomposition, while for microalgal biomass, it includes the decomposition of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and other intracellular organic compounds. In this region, the generated volatile species are not expected to interact strongly with the iron-rich mineral phase; therefore, the effect of Badar stone on the overall mass loss behavior remains limited.

In the MTZ, continued decomposition of thermally stable biomass-derived components, char formation, and secondary transformation of residual organics may overlap with the onset of OC associated reactions. The difference TG curves presented in Figure S.4 of the Supporting Information show that the deviations from the corresponding biomass-only controls were feedstock dependent and generally nonmonotonic with Badar stone loading. Although the differences remained relatively limited for several Badar stone mixtures, more pronounced negative deviations, indicating greater net mass loss relative to the biomass-only controls, were observed for some synthetic Fe2O3 mixtures. Accordingly, the relatively limited variation in the fitted apparent activation energies with Badar stone loading should not be interpreted as the absence of mineral-assisted reactions. Rather, the fitted parameters represent the combined response of unresolved biomass-derived and OC associated processes. This interpretation is supported by separate TG-DTA tests with representative gas fuels, in which CO and H2 began to react near 800 K, whereas CH4 required a higher activation temperature, as shown in Figure .

Since the majority of devolatilization takes place below these temperatures, the influence of OC loading on the net TG response remained comparatively limited in the LTZ and much of the MTZ under the present experimental conditions, resulting in nearly identical apparent activation energy values among all biomass types, with differences observed only in the fitted solid allocation α in the LTZ, as shown in Figure b for lignocellulosic-based biomass and Figure d for microalgal-based biomass. Therefore, the mass loss observed in the LTZ and most of the MTZ is interpreted as being mainly governed by biomass pyrolysis and associated devolatilization reactions, as schematically represented by Reaction R1 . Due to the absence of in situ gas analysis, the following interpretations are discussed as plausible reaction pathways rather than definitive mechanisms.

In the HTZ, the effect of the OC ratio becomes observable but remains secondary to the intrinsic properties of the biomass-derived char. The detailed kinetics data are available in Tables S.2 to S.4 in the Supporting Information. In the HTZ, the observed behavior is likely influenced by heterogeneous interactions between char, pyrolysis-derived gases, and the OC. The following reactions are therefore presented as plausible overall pathways that may contribute in this temperature range, rather than as directly verified individual mechanisms under the present TGA conditions.

These reactions are used to support the discussion of possible high-temperature interactions, but they should not be interpreted as directly verified individual mechanisms under the present experimental conditions. Since the biomass TG DTA tests were conducted under N2 without in situ gas analysis, the formation and consumption of H2, CO, CO2, CH4, and other volatile species were not directly quantified. Thus, the HTZ discussion focuses on apparent kinetic trends and feedstock-dependent behavior rather than direct product formation or oxygen carrier conversion.

For RH, the apparent activation energy in the HTZ remains relatively insensitive to the increase in Badar stone ratio, with a sum of fitted apparent activation energies of 372.3 kJ/mol at a 0.5 ratio, 367.1 kJ/mol at a 1:1 ratio, and 369.5 kJ/mol at a 2:1 ratio. This weak sensitivity reflects the dominant influence of the exceptionally high ash content of RH (33.03%), which is primarily silica-rich and leads to impeded contact between the OC and the char surface. Such behavior is consistent with the findings of Wu et al., who reported that increasing OC flow rate initially reduces carbon deposition but may result in diminishing returns at higher loadings. One possible explanation is that the exceptionally high ash content of RH, particularly its silica-rich mineral fraction, may restrict effective contact or transport between the residual carbonaceous phase and the OC. Such ash-related effects could contribute to the limited sensitivity of the apparent HTZ response to increasing OC loading, although direct confirmation would require complementary structural and microstructural characterization. Consequently, increasing the Badar stone ratio does not appear to markedly reduce the energetic barrier for char–OC interaction. A higher α value indicates that, within the present fitted sequential model, a larger fraction of the intermediate solid is allocated to the solid-forming branch of the corresponding step, rather than to volatile release. Accordingly, α2 in the HTZ should be interpreted as an apparent model parameter reflecting how the residual solid is distributed within the fitted reaction scheme, not as a direct experimental measurement of the fraction of char physically reacting with the OC. For RH, α2 exhibits only modest fluctuations, with values of 0.927, 0.933, and 0.925 for the 0.5, 1:1, and 2:1 ratios, respectively. This near invariance of α2 indicates that the amount of solid capable of progressing through the HTZ reaction step remains constrained by ash-induced structural limitations, despite variations in OC loading.

For SD, a markedly different trend is observed. Owing to its very low ash content (4.99%) and high volatile matter fraction (77.66%), the activation energy in the HTZ increases with increasing Badar stone ratio, rising from 363.4 to 371.1 kJ/mol, and then to 387.5 kJ/mol. This trend contrasts with the results reported by Xu et al., who found that increasing the OC ratio reduced the activation energy. The discrepancy can be attributed to differences in OC composition, as the Fe2O3-rich sludge ash used by Xu et al. contained alkaline-earth and alkali-metal species, such as CaO and K2O. These species are known to promote catalytic pyrolysis of solid fuels. In the present case, increasing the OC ratio for SD results in a pronounced decrease in the fitted solid allocation parameter α2, from 0.95 to 0.85. This reduction in α2 indicates that, within the present sequential fitting model, a smaller fraction of the intermediate is mathematically allocated to the solid-retaining branch of the HTZ step as the Badar stone ratio increases. This fitted trend should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of physical solid participation or OC utilization.

For SW, the response to increasing the Badar stone ratio is more balanced. SW exhibits moderate ash content (5.17%) and relatively high fixed carbon (18.28%), resulting in a char structure that is both accessible and structurally resilient. The apparent activation energy in the HTZ increases only slightly, from 365.6 kJ/mol at a 0.5 ratio to 366.6 kJ/mol at a 1:1 ratio, and 367.6 kJ/mol at a 2:1 ratio, indicating that the intrinsic char structure governs the energetic barrier rather than OC loading. In contrast to RH and SD, the fitted solid allocation parameter α2 increases modestly from approximately 0.93 to 0.97, indicating that, within the present fitted sequential model, a larger fraction of the intermediate is allocated to the solid-retaining pathway as OC loading increases. The present TG data alone do not establish whether this trend arises from changes in physical solid accessibility, oxygen transfer, or other overlapping processes.

For microalgal-based biomass, the HTZ behavior differs from that of lignocellulosic-based biomass, likely reflecting differences in biochemical composition and char structure. In this temperature range, the stronger sensitivity of the fitted parameters to biomass type and OC ratio suggests a larger contribution from interactions between microalgae-derived char or pyrolysis-derived gases and the OC. As shown by the HTZ kinetic parameters, the apparent activation energy and fitted solid allocation parameter α2 exhibit pronounced sensitivity to biomass type and OC ratio, in contrast to the relatively invariant behavior observed for lignocellulosic-based biomass.

For lipid-rich MA, the ΣEa HTZ remains within a relatively narrow range when Badar stone is used, with values of 321.6 kJ/mol at a 0.5 ratio, 327.9 kJ/mol at a 1:1 ratio, and 317.6 kJ/mol at a 2:1 ratio. No monotonic trend with increasing OC ratio is observed. This indicates that, for lipid-rich microalgae, increasing Badar stone loading does not systematically reduce the energetic barrier of HTZ reactions. The relatively low and stable apparent activation energy indicates limited sensitivity of the net HTZ response to increasing Badar stone loading. This behavior may be associated with differences in the thermal decomposition products and residual carbonaceous structure of the lipid-rich feedstock, although the underlying structural origin cannot be established from the present TG data alone. Meanwhile, α2 increases monotonically with increasing Badar stone ratio, rising from 0.771 at a 0.5 ratio, to 0.899 at a 1:1 ratio, and further to 0.929 at a 2:1 ratio. This trend suggests that, within the present sequential fitting model, a larger fraction of the residual solid is assigned to the HTZ solid reaction pathway as the Badar stone ratio increases. The relatively low initial α2 at lower Badar ratios may reflect limited apparent interaction between the residual solid and the OC, whereas the higher α2 values at larger ratios indicate a broader modeled contribution of the solid phase in the HTZ. When Fe2O3 is used, α2 decreases to 0.836, indicating that carrier mineralogy influences the extent of solid participation even when the overall oxygen availability is comparable.

In the case of ME, the ΣEa HTZ exhibits a nonmonotonic response to the Badar stone ratio. The activation energy increases from 318.1 kJ/mol at a 0.5 ratio to 345 kJ/mol at a 1:1 ratio, before decreasing to 325 kJ/mol at a 2:1 ratio. This intermediate maximum may indicate a temporary increase in the apparent resistance of the HTZ process at the intermediate ratio. One possible explanation is a change in local contact conditions between the residual solid and the OC at the intermediate loading. Previous studies have reported passivation-related behavior in microalgae–iron systems; however, the present TG data do not provide direct evidence that the same mechanism occurs here. Accordingly, the observed intermediate maximum is interpreted only as a nonmonotonic apparent kinetic response whose structural origin requires complementary characterization. Within the multistep framework, this behavior reflects a redistribution of reacting solid among intermediate states rather than a reduction in overall reactivity, consistent with temporary passivation phenomena reported in microalgae–iron systems. ME shows a declining trend in α2 with increasing Badar stone ratio. The fitted solid allocation parameter decreases from 0.906 at a 0.5 ratio to 0.897 at a 1:1 ratio and further to 0.858 at a 2:1 ratio, with a comparable value of 0.853 observed for the Fe2O3 case. This reduction in α2 implies that, although OC loading increases, a smaller fraction of the solid matrix remains able to proceed through the HTZ reaction pathway.

MS displays the highest fitted HTZ apparent activation energy among the investigated microalgal biomasses, indicating a comparatively more resistant net high-temperature mass-change response. This behavior may be associated with the characteristics of protein-rich biomass-derived residues, as previously reported in related systems, although the present TG data alone do not directly establish the corresponding char structure or reaction mechanism. The sum of fitted apparent activation energies decreases from 434.6 kJ/mol at a 0.5 ratio to 416.2 kJ/mol at a 1:1 ratio, but increases again to 453 kJ/mol at a 2:1 ratio, indicating a nonlinear response to OC loading. This behavior suggests that moderate Badar stone addition is associated with a lower apparent activation energy in the HTZ, whereas further increases in the OC ratio do not maintain this trend. This may reflect changes in the apparent accessibility or reactivity of the residual solid, but a definitive structural explanation is beyond the scope of the present TGA data set. Similar trends are evident in Wang et al., where microalgae with high protein fractions formed stable aromatic residues that required higher activation energies for oxidation and reduction. MS exhibits consistently high α2 values across all OC ratios, ranging from 0.862 to 0.884. The relatively invariant α2 indicates that a large fraction of protein-derived char remains structurally accessible for HTZ reactions regardless of carrier type or loading. This behavior suggests that, for protein-rich microalgae, the limitation in HTZ arises primarily from the energetic difficulty of breaking highly aromatic char structures, as reflected in the elevated activation energies, rather than from restricted solid participation.

sec.title: Comparison with Synthetic Fe2O3
sec.p: A direct comparison between synthetic Fe2O3 (Wako Pure Chemical Industries, Ltd., 99.9%) and Badar stone at an identical 1:1 OC-to-biomass ratio reveals systematic differences in HTZ behavior across both lignocellulosic- and microalgal-based biomasses, as shown in Figures and , respectively. In this comparison, the activation energy is interpreted as an apparent energetic barrier obtained from the fitted TG response, while α is interpreted as a fitted solid allocation parameter within the two-step model.

caption.p: Comparison of kinetic parameters for lignocellulosic-based biomass using Badar stone and synthetic Fe2O3, showing (a) activation energy and (b) fitted solid allocation parameter α.

sec.p: For lignocellulosic biomass, the use of synthetic Fe2O3 generally results in a lower sum of fitted apparent activation energy in the HTZ than Badar stone, but is accompanied by a reduction in the fitted solid allocation parameter α2. In RH, the sum of fitted apparent activation energy decreases from 368.1 kJ/mol with Badar stone to 358.3 kJ/mol with Fe2O3, while α2 declines from 0.933 to 0.913. This behavior indicates that although the energetic barrier for the dominant HTZ reaction is slightly reduced, a smaller fraction of the solid participates in the reaction pathway when synthetic Fe2O3 is employed. The effect is more pronounced for SW, where the sum of fitted apparent activation energies decreases from 366.6 to 356.4 kJ/mol, but α2 decreases from 0.954 to 0.816, suggesting restricted solid participation despite lower apparent energetic requirements. For SD, synthetic Fe2O3 yields a substantially lower sum of fitted apparent activation energy (307.2 kJ/mol) compared to Badar stone (371.1 kJ/mol), while α2 decreases from 0.906 to 0.890, indicating that the reduction in activation energy does not directly translate into broader char participation.

These trends may reflect differences in the apparent reduction behavior of synthetic Fe2O3 and Badar stone. Synthetic Fe2O3 may undergo sharper stepwise transitions (Fe2O3→Fe3O4→FeO→Fe), which could promote the temporary formation of denser intermediate layers and a more localized reaction front, as also discussed by Wang et al. In contrast, the heterogeneous mineral composition of Badar stone may distribute the redox process over a broader temperature range. As a result, although Fe2O3 may exhibit lower intrinsic activation energy for specific reduction steps, the formation of compact intermediate layers restricts oxygen transport and limits the fraction of solid that can effectively react in the HTZ. In contrast, Badar stone contains a complex mineral matrix dominated by iron (59.7% Fe), with minor but non-negligible amounts of Si (1.61%), Al, Ca, Mg, and trace transition metals. This interpretation is further supported by ex situ XRD analysis of the reduced samples obtained from RH-based experiments (Figure S.6). The diffraction patterns show that synthetic Fe2O3 exhibits more pronounced metallic Fe peaks under comparable temperature-programmed conditions, indicating faster reduction. In contrast, Badar stone retains mixed iron oxide phases (Fe3O4 and FeO), suggesting a more gradual reduction behavior within the same experimental time window. This difference is likely influenced by the limited reaction time in the nonisothermal TGA protocol, in which the experiment was terminated while the sample remained at an elevated temperature and the char–OC reaction was still progressing. Interestingly, metallic Fe formation is already observed at lower Badar loading (0.5 ratio), whereas higher Badar ratios retain stronger oxide signatures, indicating that larger OC amounts require longer reaction time to achieve complete reduction under the present conditions. These results collectively indicate that oxygen carrier performance in BDCL cannot be evaluated solely on the basis of intrinsic reduction kinetics, as mineralogical heterogeneity and biomass-dependent interactions play equally critical roles in determining overall solid participation and reaction pathways.

For microalgal-based biomass, similar but composition-dependent trends are observed as shown in Figure . In MA, the sum of fitted apparent HTZ activation energy increases from 328 kJ/mol with Badar stone to 359.3 kJ/mol with Fe2O3, while α2 decreases from 0.899 to 0.836. This indicates that synthetic Fe2O3 imposes a higher energetic penalty and reduces the fraction of lipid-derived char able to participate in HTZ reactions. ME exhibits a smaller difference in the sum of fitted apparent activation energy (345 kJ/mol for Badar stone versus 334.6 kJ/mol for Fe2O3), accompanied by a slight decrease in α2 from 0.897 to 0.853, suggesting comparable energetic barriers but more limited solid accessibility with Fe2O3. For MS, both OCs yield similarly high ΣEa (416.2 kJ/mol for Badar stone and 429.3 kJ/mol for Fe2O3). At the same time, α2 remains high but consistently lower for Fe2O3 (0.858) than for Badar stone (0.884), suggesting that protein-derived char remains intrinsically refractory regardless of carrier type. Still, solid participation is more effectively sustained by Badar stone.

caption.p: Comparison of kinetic parameters for microalgal-based biomass using Badar stone and synthetic Fe2O3, showing (a) activation energy and (b) fitted solid allocation parameter α.

sec.p: It should be noted that the lower α2 values obtained for synthetic Fe2O3 do not necessarily indicate lower intrinsic reactivity. In the separate TG–DTA tests with CO, CH4, and H2, as shown in Figure , synthetic Fe2O3 showed faster apparent reduction behavior than Badar stone. Within the present fitting framework, this may correspond to a narrower modeled distribution of the reacting solid in the HTZ. However, the exact mechanistic basis of this behavior cannot be directly established without complementary characterization. Within the sequential multistep framework, this behavior concentrates the reaction into a narrower fraction of the solid matrix, thereby reducing the overall fraction of solid that progresses through the HTZ reaction pathway and manifests as a lower α2 value. In contrast, Badar stone undergoes reduction more gradually due to its heterogeneous mineral composition, which includes iron as the dominant phase together with Si, Al, Ca, Mg, and trace transition metals. This distributed reduction behavior delays the formation of dense reduced layers and promotes a more spatially uniform reaction front. As a result, a larger fraction of the solid matrix participates in HTZ reactions, yielding higher α2 values despite slower overall reduction rates. Therefore, the main advantage of Badar stone in the present study is not its higher intrinsic reactivity than synthetic Fe2O3, but its distinct, more gradual high-temperature response as a low-cost, natural, iron-rich mineral. Further gas analysis, cyclic redox experiments, and postreaction characterization are needed to determine whether this broader TG response can translate into practical oxygen-carrier performance in biomass chemical-looping systems.

sec.title: Scope and Limitations
sec.p: The present study provides a comparative TG-DTA-based screening of biomass and iron-rich mineral mixtures under chemical looping-relevant thermal conditions. The analysis clarifies how different biomass feedstocks influence devolatilization, residual solid formation, and apparent high-temperature interaction with Badar stone and synthetic Fe2O3. However, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results.

First, the biomass and mineral mixture experiments were conducted under N2 without in situ gas analysis. Therefore, the formation and consumption of H2, CO, CO2, CH4, tar, and other volatile species were not directly quantified. The reactions involving pyrolysis-derived gases, residual char, and the oxygen carrier are therefore discussed as plausible pathways based on TG-DTA trends and previous literature, rather than as directly verified individual reaction mechanisms. The measured TG signal represents the net result of simultaneous mass loss and possible mass gain phenomena. Depending on biomass composition and OC loading, devolatilization, char conversion, oxygen carrier reduction, secondary reactions of pyrolysis-derived species, carbon deposition, and mineral transformations may overlap within the same temperature interval. Because carbon deposition was not independently quantified, its contribution cannot be separated from the other processes based on TG data alone. Therefore, the fitted kinetic parameters should be interpreted as apparent comparative descriptors of the overall thermogravimetric response under identical experimental conditions rather than as isolated kinetic constants of individual reactions.

Second, the kinetic parameters obtained from the multistep model should be interpreted as apparent parameters under the selected nonisothermal condition. The model was applied to reproduce the measured TG profiles in the LTZ, MTZ, and HTZ, and it successfully captured the overall mass-loss behavior. Nevertheless, the fitted activation energy values do not represent intrinsic kinetic constants of elementary reactions. Similarly, the fitted parameter α represents the mathematical allocation of intermediate material to the solid retaining pathway in the sequential model. It should not be interpreted as a direct experimental measurement of physical solid participation, char conversion, or oxygen carrier utilization.

Third, the LTZ, MTZ, and HTZ were defined as empirical fitting windows based on distinct regions of the measured TG and DTG profiles. Although these temperature windows overlap with ranges reported for biomass decomposition and stepwise iron oxide reduction, they should not be interpreted as mechanistically exclusive reaction regimes or as one-to-one assignments of individual reduction steps. Multiple physicochemical processes may occur simultaneously within each temperature window.

Fourth, the comparison between the Badar stone and synthetic Fe2O3 should be understood as a screening-level comparison between a heterogeneous, natural, iron-rich mineral and a chemically uniform synthetic oxide. Synthetic Fe2O3 generally showed sharper apparent high-temperature reactivity, whereas Badar stone exhibited broader, more gradual high-temperature behavior. However, the current data are insufficient to determine whether this broader behavior directly translates into higher oxygen transfer capacity, better cyclic stability, or improved reactor-scale performance.

In addition, the TG signal represents the net result of simultaneous mass-loss and possible mass-gain phenomena. Depending on biomass composition and OC loading, biomass devolatilization, char conversion, oxygen carrier reduction, secondary cracking, and carbon deposition may overlap within the same temperature interval. Therefore, the present kinetic parameters should be interpreted as apparent descriptors of the net thermogravimetric response under identical comparative conditions rather than as isolated kinetic constants of individual reactions.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This work investigated the initial kinetics of lignocellulosic and microalgal biomass in a direct chemical looping process with volcanic-based natural metal oxides, using a mass-balance-based multistep kinetic model. Rice husk, sawdust, sago waste, and three types of microalgae were employed as representative biomass feedstocks, while natural Badar stone and synthetic Fe2O3 were used as OCs. The thermal decomposition behavior, reaction step structure, kinetic parameters, and solid and gas evolution characteristics were systematically analyzed based on TG and DTG measurements. The main conclusions are summarized as follows.

list-item.p: TG and DTG analyses showed that devolatilization of both lignocellulosic- and microalgal-based biomasses occurred mainly at 700–800 K and was largely independent of OC type. Lignocellulosic-based biomass followed typical hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin degradation, whereas microalgal-based biomass exhibited patterns governed by lipid, carbohydrate, and protein contents. The OC had a limited influence on volatile release but a greater influence on the apparent high-temperature response above 950 K.

A three-zone temperature framework comprising 400–800, 800–1000, and 1000–1300 K was introduced as a practical segmentation of the TG and DTG profiles. When combined with the two-step sequential fitting model applied within each zone, this approach reproduced the experimental curves with fitting values generally above 99%.

In the LTZ and MTZ, activation energies showed minimal sensitivity to OC ratio for all biomass types, suggesting the dominance of biomass pyrolysis and the limited involvement of heterogeneous redox reactions.

In the HTZ, biomass-dependent kinetic behavior became pronounced. Lignocellulosic-based biomass showed weak sensitivity to the OC ratio due to char structure and ash effects, whereas microalgal-based biomass kinetics were strongly governed by biochemical composition, with lipid-rich biomass exhibiting lower activation energies and protein-rich biomass showing higher values.

At an identical 1:1 ratio, synthetic Fe2O3 showed faster apparent reduction behavior than Badar stone in the comparative TG-DTA tests, whereas the fitted α values in the HTZ were generally lower. Within the present model framework, this suggests a narrower apparent distribution of the reacting solid for Fe2O3 than for Badar stone, although direct mechanistic confirmation requires complementary characterization.

The different trends of apparent activation energy and fitted α values in the HTZ indicate that these parameters describe different aspects of the sequential fitting model and should not be interpreted independently as direct measures of intrinsic reactivity or overall conversion.

sec.p: Although the kinetic parameters were derived from temperature-programmed chemical looping experiments, the conclusions provide mechanistic insights relevant to isothermal chemical looping systems as well. Further investigation is required to validate the Badar stone as an oxygen carrier for biomass chemical looping applications. In situ evolved gas analysis is needed to quantify H2, CO, CO2, CH4, and other gaseous products. Postreaction XRD and SEM-EDS analyses are necessary to confirm phase transformation, ash-mineral interactions, and surface-morphology changes after the reaction. Cyclic redox tests are also required to evaluate oxygen transfer capacity, reactivity retention, agglomeration tendency, and long-term stability. Therefore, the present work should be regarded as an initial screening study that identifies feedstock-dependent thermal and kinetic behavior and provides a basis for selecting representative biomass and mineral combinations for subsequent validation.
